review.notes: Built on the course: true demand, stock-out cleaning, promotions, WMA, exponential smoothing, seasonal index, error = forecast - actual, MAD, bias, tracking signal, FVA, lag measurement, time fences, S&OP steps. Calculations checked. Fictional company.

content.company: Baylight Foods (fictional), importing rice, oil and canned goods with a 3-month lead time
content.briefing: Sales say the forecast is always wrong, finance says stock is too high, and the warehouse runs out of best-sellers. You own the forecast and the monthly S&OP cycle. Make the numbers trusted again.

variants.text: In March, oil sold 300 cases, but stock ran out for 10 of 30 days. On days with stock it sold 15 a day. What was true demand?

choices.f: 15 x 30 days. Shipments miss lost sales; you flag the adjustment.
That is what was shipped, capped by the stock-out.
You scaled the wrong way. Demand was higher, not lower.

variants.text: A huge spike in May came from a one-off promotion. What do you do with it in the history?

choices.t: Separate the promotion from the baseline
choices.f: The baseline stays clean; promotions are forecast separately.

choices.t: Leave it; it is real sales
choices.f: Next May's forecast will expect the spike again.
You lose the normal demand inside it too.

variants.text: Last three months: 100, 120, 140 cases. Weights 0.2, 0.3, 0.5 (most recent last). Weighted moving average?

choices.f: Correct: 20 + 36 + 70.
That is the simple average.
You put the biggest weight on the oldest month.

variants.text: Exponential smoothing, alpha 0.3. Old forecast 180, actual 200. New forecast?

choices.f: You swapped alpha: 0.7 x 200 + 0.3 x 180.
That is the naive forecast, not smoothing.

variants.text: December averages 150 cases; the overall monthly average is 100. What is December's seasonal index?

choices.f: Correct: 150 / 100. December sells 50% above an average month.
You divided the wrong way.
That is the difference, not the index.

variants.text: A fancy new model beats nothing in tests. Before trusting it, what do you compare it with?

choices.f: If a model cannot beat 'next month = last month', it adds no value.
Opinions are another step to test, not the baseline.
Complex is not always more accurate.

variants.text: Errors (forecast minus actual) for three months: +10, -20, +30. What is the MAD?

choices.f: That uses signed errors. MAD uses absolute values.
That is the total, not the average.

variants.text: Forecast 120, actual 100. Using the course rule, what is the error?

choices.f: Error = forecast - actual. Positive means you over-forecast.
Sign reversed. Forecast was above actual.
That is a percentage error, not the error in units.

variants.text: Cumulative error over six months is +60; MAD is 20. What is the tracking signal?

choices.f: Correct: 60 / 20. A steady positive value shows a bias to over-forecast.
You multiplied. Divide by MAD.
You divided the wrong way.

variants.text: A slow item sold 10 against a forecast of 20. Its MAPE looks terrible. What do you tell management?

choices.t: Small items inflate MAPE; check units too
choices.f: A 10-unit miss is 100% here but tiny in value.

choices.t: Fire the planner for this item
choices.f: The percentage misleads on small volumes.
They still need a plan, with the right measure.

variants.text: Statistical forecast error: 18%. After sales adjustments: 24%. What does forecast value added show?

choices.t: Sales input made it worse here
choices.f: Keep steps that reduce error; review those that add it.
Here it raised the error by 6 points.
Comparing steps is exactly what FVA does.

variants.text: Lead time is 3 months. Which forecast do you judge accuracy on?

choices.t: The one made when the order was placed
choices.f: Lag 3: that forecast drove the purchase.
Too late to change what was ordered.

choices.t: The best forecast of the year
choices.f: Cherry-picking hides real performance.

variants.text: Rice: forecast over lead time plus review 2,400 bags, safety stock 400, on hand 900, on order 1,100. Net requirement?

choices.f: Correct: 2,400 + 400 - 900 - 1,100. Then round to full containers.
You ignored stock on hand and on order.
You forgot stock on order.

variants.text: Your net requirement is 800 bags, but a container holds 1,000. The supplier minimum is one container.

choices.t: Round up to one full container
choices.f: Constraints apply after the net calculation.
Below the supplier minimum; the order is refused.
You run out before the next order arrives.

variants.text: Sales wants to change a shipment already loaded on the vessel. Which fence?

choices.f: Loaded or paid means frozen.
Slushy is ordered but not yet loaded.
Liquid is beyond the ordering horizon.

variants.text: An order is placed but not loaded. Sales wants to swap one product. Which fence and rule?

choices.f: Possible, with cost and supplier agreement.
Not loaded yet, so not frozen.
Already ordered, so not liquid.

variants.text: In what order do the S&OP steps run each month?

choices.f: Each step feeds the next and ends in one plan.
Executives decide on prepared options.
Demand is agreed before supply can respond.

variants.text: In pre-S&OP, demand exceeds the supply plan for oil in Q4. What do you prepare?

choices.f: Extra vessel, rationing, or price action. Executives decide.

choices.t: Lower the demand plan to fit supply
choices.f: That hides the gap instead of solving it.

choices.t: Wait to see what happens in Q4
choices.f: Lead time is 3 months; waiting means stock-outs.

variants.text: At which level do you plan vessels and cash for the next 12 months?

choices.f: Families for capacity and cash; SKUs for purchase orders.
Too much detail for a 12-month view.
Too broad to plan vessels and products.

variants.text: Powdered milk is C value and Z (erratic). How much effort do you put into its forecast?

choices.t: Little: simple rules or buy to order
choices.f: Spend effort on A and X items where it pays.

choices.t: Most: erratic items need complex models
choices.f: Erratic, low-value items rarely repay the effort.
One effort level for all wastes planner time.
